title: Proving Greedy Correct — The Exchange Argument
summary: The general proof technique for showing a greedy choice is safe to make, worked through concretely on interval scheduling.

slides.markdown:
The exchange argument is the standard technique for proving that a greedy choice is safe — that locking it in now can never prevent reaching a globally optimal solution. It has the same two-step shape every time, regardless of which specific problem you're applying it to.

This matters beyond passing a whiteboard proof: it's the difference between "I think this greedy works" and "I can show this greedy works," and interviewers routinely ask for exactly that distinction once you propose a greedy strategy. `greedy-fundamentals` showed *why* proof matters (the coin-change trap); this topic gives you the actual tool.

slides.subTitle: Assume an optimal solution that disagrees
slides.markdown:
Start by assuming, for contradiction, that some optimal solution `O` exists that does **not** make the same choice your greedy strategy would make at the first point of disagreement. This is a standard proof setup — you're not trying to show your greedy solution is optimal directly; you're trying to show that *any* optimal solution can be transformed into one that agrees with greedy, without becoming worse.

Concretely, for activity selection: assume `O` is an optimal set of non-overlapping activities, and that `O`'s first choice isn't the earliest-finishing activity your greedy strategy would pick. Call greedy's first pick `g` and `O`'s actual first pick `o`.

slides.subTitle: Show the swap can't make things worse
slides.markdown:
Swap `o` out of `O` and put `g` in its place, producing a new solution `O'`. Show two things: `O'` is still valid (no new conflicts introduced), and `O'` is at least as good as `O` (same size, same or better value, depending on the objective).

For activity selection: because `g` finishes no later than `o` (that's what "earliest-finishing" means), everything in `O` that came after `o` is still compatible with `g` — `g` frees up at least as much room as `o` did. So `O'` is still a valid non-overlapping set, with the same count as `O`. Since `O` was assumed optimal and `O'` is at least as good, `O'` is also optimal — and now it agrees with greedy's first choice.

Picture an optimal schedule as a row of chosen intervals. One of them, `o`, is replaced by `g` — an interval that finishes no later than `o` and starts no earlier than the previous chosen interval's end.

<<< Image: a row of 4 non-overlapping intervals on a timeline representing an optimal solution O, with one interval labelled "o" circled; below it, the same row with "o" replaced by a slightly-shorter, earlier-finishing interval labelled "g", with the remaining intervals unchanged and still non-overlapping, captioned "same count, still valid, now agrees with greedy" >>>

Every other chosen interval in the row is untouched by the swap — that's the point: the exchange is local and surgical, not a wholesale reshuffling of the whole solution.

Written as a proof sketch rather than code, but structured exactly like an algorithm:

```text
Claim: earliest-finish-time greedy is optimal for activity selection.

Proof by exchange argument:
1. Let O be any optimal solution, g = greedy's first pick (earliest finish
   among all activities), o = O's first pick.
2. finish(g) <= finish(o), by definition of g.
3. Replace o with g in O, forming O'.
4. Every activity in O after o started at or after finish(o) >= finish(g),
   so it's still compatible with g. O' is valid.
5. |O'| = |O|, so O' is also optimal, and now agrees with greedy on the
   first choice.
6. Repeat inductively on the remaining subproblem (activities compatible
   with g) to show full agreement.
```

Step 6 is the optimal-substructure step, covered next — the exchange argument alone only handles the *first* choice; induction extends it to every choice.

The exchange argument alone only proves that greedy's *first* choice is safe. To conclude the *entire* greedy strategy is optimal, you need one more piece: **the remaining problem, after removing the chosen element and everything it conflicts with, is the same problem, just smaller.**

For activity selection: once `g` is chosen, the remaining activities (those compatible with `g`) form a smaller instance of exactly the same activity-selection problem. Applying the exchange argument again to *that* smaller instance justifies greedy's second choice, and so on inductively. Without this step, you've only shown "the first choice is safe" — not "the whole strategy, repeated, is safe." Both pieces — greedy-choice property (the exchange argument) and optimal substructure (the shrinking-subproblem step) — are required together, exactly as `greedy-fundamentals` introduced.

| | Exchange argument | Stays-ahead proof |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | Take any optimal solution, swap in the greedy choice, show no harm | Show greedy's partial progress is always at least as good as any other strategy's partial progress, at every prefix |
| Feels like | "I can always substitute greedy's pick without losing anything" | "Greedy is never behind, checkpoint by checkpoint" |
| Common for | Selection/scheduling problems (activity selection, Huffman) | Problems with a natural notion of running progress (some scheduling and matching problems) |

Both are standard templates for greedy correctness proofs, and some problems admit either one. Exchange argument is the more broadly applicable default to reach for first; stays-ahead is worth knowing exists as an alternative framing if the exchange framing feels awkward for a specific problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Showing 'a valid answer,' not 'the optimal one'
slides.markdown:
A common proof mistake: showing that the swapped solution `O'` is still a *valid* non-overlapping set (no conflicts), and stopping there — without separately confirming `O'` is *at least as good as* `O` (same or better count/value). Validity and optimality are two different claims, and a proof sketch that only establishes the first has proven nothing about correctness.

For activity selection this second check is easy (`|O'| = |O|`, same count, since it's a like-for-like swap), but for problems where the objective is a sum or a more complex quantity, this step needs actual justification — you have to show the swap doesn't *decrease* the objective, not just that it doesn't break any constraints. Skipping this is the single most common way an exchange-argument sketch looks complete while actually proving nothing.

slides.sectionTitle: When no exchange argument presents itself
slides.markdown:
If you genuinely try to construct an exchange argument and keep finding that swapping in the locally-best choice *can* make things worse — that a counterexample keeps surfacing no matter how you adjust the strategy — treat that as a real signal, not a proof-writing skill issue. It usually means the problem doesn't have the greedy-choice property at all, and you should pivot to DP.

This is the practical version of the coin-change lesson from `greedy-fundamentals`: the failed proof attempt *is* the diagnostic. Spending five minutes trying to sketch an exchange argument, even informally, is a fast and reliable way to decide between a greedy approach and a DP approach before committing to writing either one's full code.

In an interview, you rarely need the full formal write-up — you need a compressed version that signals you *could* produce the full proof. The compressed version has three beats: **(1)** name the greedy choice, **(2)** state the swap ("if an optimal solution didn't make this choice, I can always substitute it in"), **(3)** state why the swap doesn't hurt ("...because it finishes no later, so it can't conflict with anything the rest of the optimal solution kept").

Saying those three sentences, unprompted, right after proposing a greedy strategy is usually enough to fully satisfy an interviewer that you're not just guessing — it's a small amount of talking that signals a large amount of understanding.

slides.sectionTitle: The template you'll reuse all group
slides.markdown:
Every remaining problem in this group — Jump Game's reachability argument, Gas Station's reset rule, Huffman's tree-depth argument — is an exchange argument wearing different clothes. The specific quantity being swapped changes (an interval, a jump target, a starting index, a symbol's tree position), but the shape doesn't: assume an optimal alternative disagrees, show the swap is safe, invoke shrinking optimal substructure to extend it to every choice.

Carrying this template forward is the actual payoff of spending a full topic on it — you'll recognize the shape faster in each new problem instead of re-deriving proof technique from scratch every time.
